Diane Taylor is a Guardian reporter who covers migration.

Britons get many of the facts about migration wrong and Reform UK voters are the group who get these facts most wrong, according to new research published today by King’s College University and YouGov.

Among Reform UK supporters, 57% think net migration rose significantly in the year to June 2025, compared with 11% of Labour supporters and 8% of Greens. Eight in 10 Reform supporters think that asylum seekers are prioritised for social housing, compared with 21% of Green supporters.

It is wrong to believe that if we could only correct misperceptions, we would automatically reduce concerns about immigration or policy preferences – because that misdiagnoses a large part of the cause, that these divides are partly driven by deep differences in values and identity.

items.title: A few questions for the guy who went snorkeling in a Home Depot retention pond
items.summary:
Joseph Ricketts in the retention pond. | Joseph Ricketts 

One night earlier this fall, a biologist and YouTuber in Florida named Joseph Ricketts went snorkeling in a retention pond next to his local Home Depot. 

He filmed what he saw and posted a video to his channel titled “ Night Snorkel In a Home Depot Retention Pond .” It quickly blew up, hitting more than 2 million views as of this writing, and for good reason: It’s not at all what you might expect.

Ricketts found an aquatic world teeming with life on his dive into what is, from the surface, a stagnant pool of water filled with old beer cans. A water snake undulated through the pond, a bulge in its stomach revealing a recent meal. Tadpoles darted about, some of them half on their way to froghood. Mysterious shrimp scuttled along the silty bottom.

Ricketts, who works as a crocodile and alligator research biologist in Florida, went for his first snorkeling trip when he was 16 years old. On that trip, he came face-to-face with a manatee — and was instantly hooked. “I experienced so much joy in that moment, and I just kind of subconsciously knew I’d be chasing that for the rest of my life to some degree or another,” he told me. 

Ricketts still takes a lot of joy in snorkeling, in part because of how it allows him to quickly access a totally different world hiding just under the surface of the water; his YouTube bio declares, “I’ll snorkel pretty much anywhere.” And his recent retention pond dive among the suburban detritus bears that out. 

I talked with Ricketts recently about urban ecology, snorkeling, and what…
items.t: A few questions for the guy who went snorkeling in a Home Depot retention pond

items.title: HIV was supposed to kill them. Now they could help scientists find a cure.
items.summary:
This story was originally published in  The Highlight . To get access to member-exclusive stories like this every month,  become a Vox Member today . 

Paul Boakye was 22 when he was diagnosed with HIV. It was winter 1986, five years after the world first became aware of the deadly disease that would become known as acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS). After receiving the news, Boakye was certain he was going to die young. “I distinctly remember a doctor telling me that I probably wouldn’t live to see 30,” he said. 

Years passed, and Boakye watched as both his former partner and many of his friends died of complications from HIV, which infiltrates immune cells and weakens the body’s defenses. During the early days of the HIV pandemic, a diagnosis was essentially a death sentence. Without getting treatment, HIV infections can eventually develop into AIDS — the stage in which a person’s immune system has deteriorated to the point that they become vulnerable to typically harmless infections and rare cancers. Once AIDS manifests, life expectancy drops to just a few years. 

But Boakye was an exception. 

Now four decades after his diagnosis, at age 63, he remains symptom-free. He is one of the rare people with HIV whose immune systems can fight off the virus without treatment. These individuals, known as “elite controllers,” make up less than 0.5 percent of those who get infected with HIV.

For many scientists, this group of people provides a roadmap for a so-called functional cure, a state akin to cancer remission, where the infection is under control, but not…
items.t: HIV was supposed to kill them. Now they could help scientists find a cure.

items.title: Trump wants an immigration deal. He could start with caregivers.
items.summary:
This story was originally published in The Highlight . To get access to member-exclusive stories like this every month, become a Vox Member today . 

Unlike projecting how many jobs AI may eliminate over the next 10 years, or what a country’s birth rate might look like, there’s far less debate among policymakers about how large America’s older population will be in a decade’s time, and how many of them are likely to need direct care for disabilities.

By 2036, as the baby boomers continue to retire, the US population 65 and older is expected to grow from 65.6 million to 77.5 million people, according to the Congressional Budget Office. The number of people 85 and older is also expected to nearly double in that time, from 6.8 million to 11.1 million.

The question of whether the United States will have enough direct care workers — an umbrella term that refers to home health aides, personal care aides, and nursing assistants — looms large. These are workers, primarily women, who help older adults and people with disabilities bathe, dress, eat, take their medication, and generally get through a day, either in a nursing home or in someone’s own home. It’s a massive, often ignored workforce (the American Community Survey estimates there were 3.62 million of them in 2024) and it’s paid for largely by Medicaid, the joint federal-state health insurance program that most people associate with coverage for impoverished Americans but which is actually the dominant payer for long-term care in this country. 

Key takeaways 

By 2036 the US will need 625,000 to 1.3 million more direct…
items.t: Trump wants an immigration deal. He could start with caregivers.

items.title: The college Republicans who voted blue in the midterms
items.summary:
Supporters wear MAGA hats as they attend a midterm campaign rally by Vice President JD Vance in Weatherford, Texas, on October 29, 2026. | Evan Vucci/Getty Images 

For a brief, fleeting moment after the Democrats’ crushing midterm victory, President Donald Trump seemed open to moderating his approach to immigration.

Then he said psych! and named Stephen Miller, the architect of his most aggressive and controversial immigration policies, as White House chief of staff. The move seemed to signal that Trump and his coalition will be doubling down and seeking to win back base voters disaffected by the war in Iran and high cost of living with red-meat issues. But some of those voters might be too far gone.

“The fact that Stephen Miller is Jewish, they’re just like, ‘Yeah, I don’t know,’” Simon van Zuylen-Wood , a staff writer with New York magazine who has been checking in with a College Republicans chapter at Clemson University for more than a year, told Today, Explained co-host Noel King.

Counterintuitively, though, van Zuylen-Wood found that some of those same college Republicans helped power the blue wave that lifted Sen.-elect Annie Andrews (D-SC) to an upset win over Sen. Darline Graham (R-SC).

Noel and van Zuylen-Wood talked about why those Clemson Republicans chose to vote for a Democrat, how they’re nevertheless increasingly in thrall to the white nationalist podcaster Nick Fuentes, and their deep dislike of Vice President JD Vance.

Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today,…

items.title: In Waves review – love, grief and surfing at heart of profoundly moving animated tale
items.summary:
Tenderly drawn story combines a history of surfing with an emotional account of losing a partner to bone cancer aged 24

This gently moving and beautifully animated drama is adapted from an award-winning graphic novel by Californian illustrator AJ Dungo. His book combines a history of surfing with a memoir of love and grief; it is an account of his girlfriend Kristen Tuason, who died from bone cancer at just 24. There is something desperately sad in the film’s nostalgic mood: Dungo still in his 20s, already looking in the rearview at his youth like it’s a different universe.

AJ (voiced by Will Sharpe) is a gawky teenager skateboarder who meets fun, outgoing Kirsten (Stephanie Hsu); she’s a surfer and helps AJ to overcome his fear of the ocean. Pretty soon, they’re a couple, hanging out with friends, surfing with a mixtape of sunny bright pop tunes soundtracking their teenage years. Then Kirsten is diagnosed with cancer and undergoes surgery to partially amputate her leg. When the doctors tell her she’s in remission, life goes on. Kirsten trains to be a nurse, while her brother opens a surf shop; another friend starts a craft beer business; AJ is working hard at art school. Life is ahead of them.

Arguably, the film, directed by Phuong Mai Nguyen, is light on detail: characters’ facial expressions are illustrated in simple lines, the finer details of their personalities unsketched. By contrast, the ocean is rendered in spectacular depth and detail, in all its moods. There is a reverence for the…

items.title: Jensen Huang’s return takes founder worship to a dangerous level
items.summary:
The news of Jensen Huang’s resurrection at Nvidia felt like a practical joke or an Onion headline. Here was a cofounder and CEO of a trillion-dollar company who did just about all the bad things a CEO could do — including maybe involvement in espionage — who’d gotten his comeuppance. The board did its job. The investigations commenced, and Huang resigned in a rare moment of accountability in Silicon Valley culture. 

But that’s not how the story ended. Huang quickly returned to the helm of Nvidia thanks to his personal friend, the president of the United States, Donald Trump, who had pressured the board to reinstate the disgraced founder. (“I made the deal,” Trump told a television audience.) When the newly vindicated CEO walked back into Nvidia headquarters on Monday, ecstatic employees cheered his name — “Jensen! Jensen!” 

Considering the larger context, this is absurd. Huang is still under investigation at Nvidia, the company that he’s once again running, over his relationship with a tech executive, Alice Huang, who’d been talking to China’s top spy agency during the affair. And she’s under investigation over her alleged role in smuggling illegal Nvidia chips into China. 

“It’s the worst degradation in corporate governance in American history and the greatest business-government scandal in US history,” Jeffrey Sonnenfeld , the senior associate dean for leadership studies at Yale School of Management, told me a couple of hours after the news broke. “I mean, this is crazy.”

Key takeaways 

Silicon Valley’s founder worship started with a bad founder. In the 1950s, eight…
items.t: Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia takes founder worship to a dangerous level

items.title: Why the Army wants to detonate toxic explosives in Iowa
items.summary:
A sign identifying the facility sits inside a fence surrounding the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, on November 19, 2026. | Scott Olson/Getty Images 

This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day. Subscribe here .

In Iowa, the Pentagon is preparing to send a toxic plume of lead dust into the sky the day before Thanksgiving — by blowing up about five tons of lead azide, an unstable explosive, in order to dispose of it. 

The detonation was briefly halted by a lower court before a federal circuit court cleared the way on Monday, and it now appears set to take place on Wednesday morning. 

According to the Army , there’s a real need for haste: The lead azide is sufficiently unstable that it’s at risk of detonating on its own in an uncontrolled explosion, and falling temperatures in Iowa reportedly make such an explosion more likely. An uncontrolled explosion would also be more dangerous and unpredictable, and potentially cause worse lead pollution.

At the same time, though, Iowa residents are angry and alarmed by a lack of clear information, poor communication by the Army, and the potential health hazards. 

The potential for things to go sideways has President Donald Trump nervous enough that he tried to pass the decision to Rob Sand — not the current Iowa governor, but the incoming Democratic governor- elect — and let any consequences fall on his head. But as of Tuesday, it appears the detonation will go forward with court approval.

items.title: How Donald Trump warped the most important law protecting assault victims on campus
items.summary:
Protesters at a rally in support of a former Cornell University student known as Jane Doe on October 13, 2026, in Ithaca, New York. | Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images 

In the weeks since reports about an alleged gang rape at Cornell University went public, I’ve heard a lot of people ask why we haven’t made more progress on campus sexual assault. 

I understand the question. I started working on the issue as a student activist more than 15 years ago. Now, as an attorney at Public Justice, I represent student survivors of sexual assault in lawsuits against their schools. Seeing the stories out of Cornell sometimes makes me feel like nothing has changed since I was an undergraduate.

But that’s not quite right: We did make progress. Schools started taking more seriously their responsibilities to address sexual assaults, providing survivors with academic and mental health support to help them stay in school and setting up procedures to investigate allegations. This progress was spurred significantly by enforcement of Title IX, the federal law that prohibits sex discrimination in education and offers protections to student survivors of sexual assault.

However, that progress was met by backlash — both political backlash specific to Title IX and a broader hostility to civil rights in the federal courts. As a result, Title IX is now less effective in protecting student survivors than it was a decade ago. And in some ways, Title IX now effectively encourages schools to mistreat victims. What a bitter irony for a sex discrimination law.

Some of these changes, such as the Trump…
items.t: To combat sexual assault on campus, it’s time to look past Title IX

items.title: Chris Van Hollen wants to replace Chuck Schumer. We asked him why.

“We've been given this big opportunity, with 56 senators. We cannot blow it, and we need to show people that we're going to deliver and fight for them,” Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-MD), who is challenging Sen. Chuck Schumer for majority leader, said on America, Actually. | Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images 

Change is coming to Washington, DC, next Congress — and one Democratic senator thinks that that should also mean a change in leadership for the new Senate majority.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) is challenging Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-NY), who has led the party’s caucus in the upper chamber for a decade, for the top job in the new Congress. Van Hollen, who previously served in the House before being elected to the Senate in 2016, said the party needs a fresh face to deliver the change voters demanded when they handed Dems such big victories in the midterms. 

In an interview on Vox’s America, Actually podcast, Van Hollen told host Astead Herndon that Schumer has been too timid in confronting Trump and the Republican Party, and too unwilling to use unconventional means to try to rally support for Democratic causes.

“My view is that working outside the Congress to highlight the attacks on our democracy was essential. You can’t just use the same tools that were used before Trump to take on a lawless Trump,” Van Hollen said. “We need to organize in this moment to help protect our democracy and our Constitution and get things done and deliver.”

Herndon spoke with Van Hollen ahead of the December 1 vote that will decide the chamber’s Democratic leadership for the new Congress; below is…

items.title: Millions of turkeys will be thrown in the trash this Thanksgiving
items.summary:
A turkey arrives at the 2024 White House turkey pardon, a strange annual “song and dance of celebrating turkeys while we torture them,” as Vox’s Kenny Torrella put it last year. | Susan Walsh/Associated Press 

This week, tens of millions of Americans will partake in a national ritual many of us say we don’t especially enjoy or find meaning in. We will collectively eat tens of millions of turkeys , factory-farmed and heavily engineered animals that bear scant resemblance to the wild birds that have been apocryphally written into the Thanksgiving story. (The first Thanksgiving probably didn’t have turkey.) And we will do it all even though turkey meat is widely considered flavorless and unpalatable. 

“It is, almost without fail, a dried-out, depressing hunk of sun-baked papier-mâché — a jaw-tiringly chewy, unsatisfying, and depressingly bland workout,” journalist Brian McManus wrote for Vice . “Deep down, we know this, but bury it beneath happy memories of Thanksgivings past.” 

So what is essentially the national holiday of meat-eating revolves around an animal dish that no one really likes. That fact clashes with the widely accepted answer to the central question of why it’s so hard to convince everyone to ditch meat , or even to eat less of it: the taste, stupid. 

Undoubtedly, that has something to do with it. But I think the real answer is a lot more complicated, and the tasteless Thanksgiving turkey explains why. 

Inside this story 

Why Americans eat turkey on Thanksgiving, despite many of us not liking it very much! 

What life is like for a Thanksgiving turkey.…
items.t: Millions of turkeys will be thrown in the trash this Thanksgiving

items.title: Justice is elusive for the Rohingya even after the ICJ’s landmark genocide ruling against Myanmar
items.summary:
By nine votes to six, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya people in connection with its 2017 “clearance operations” in Rakhine State. The ruling is an alarm bell for all states accused of genocide.

The year 2017 was not the first Rohingya exodus from Myanmar: in 1978 and again in 1991-92, hundreds of thousands of Rohingya poured into Bangladesh to escape state persecution. Many returned, and were forced to flee again when new violence erupted.

Today, more than 1.2 million Rohingya are in refugee camps in Bangladesh without any concrete prospect to return to Myanmar. Most Rohingya want to return, but not without conditions that would ensure their safety. The most crucial condition is the guarantee of citizenship rights.

Since Myanmar stripped the Rohingya of their citizenship in 1982, they have been living under apartheid-like conditions. Among many discriminatory policies imposed on Rohingya life,…
items.t: Justice is elusive for the Rohingya even after the ICJ’s landmark genocide ruling against Myanmar

items.title: Mother tongue language rights don’t implement themselves: Lessons from Nepal’s classrooms
items.summary:
In a Grade 2 classroom in Rautahat, in Nepal’s southern plains, teacher Renuka Dahal holds up a picture card of a mango. She gives the Nepali word, then asks her students what they call it at home. They respond in Tharu and Maithili, the languages many of them speak with their families.

“I ask my students to teach me words in their language,” she told UNICEF in 2025. “It makes them feel that I care about who they are.” And that small exchange marks a real change.

For Canadians interested in Indigenous language revitalization, and for teachers welcoming newcomer students, Nepal’s experience shows what it takes to move language rights off paper and into the classroom.

For generations, many children in Nepal started school in a language they didn’t understand. Yet research shows that beginning school in a familiar language can strengthen learning and make it easier to acquire additional languages, including Nepali and English.

Nepal has written that lesson into its 2015 Constitution, which guarantees communities the right to education in their mother tongue.

items.title: The Supreme Court is about to decide if assault rifle bans can exist
items.summary:
Activists rally outside the Supreme Court before a Second Amendment case in 2023. | ﻿Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images 

On December 2, the Supreme Court will hear two cases asking whether lawmakers may ban so-called assault rifles, semiautomatic weapons equipped with various features that allow a shooter to fire many rounds with greater accuracy than if they used an ordinary rifle.

The cases involve two similar laws, one out of Cook County, Illinois and another out of Connecticut, that seek to ban civilian ownership of AR-15s, a popular gun that was used in several recent mass shootings, and similar weapons. While there are subtle differences between the two laws, both ban semiautomatic rifles with features such as pistol grips that reduce recoil and make it easier for a shooter to rapidly fire many shots at a target.

(There is a chance that the Cook County case will be declared moot , but if that happens the Court will still be able to decide the Connecticut case.)

The most striking thing about the briefs in these two cases, Viramontes v. Cook County and Grant v. Higgins , is that they describe two entirely different Second Amendments that operate in completely different ways. Yet both of these competing Second Amendments can be found in this Court’s precedents.

It’s unclear just how much the Court’s decision to choose one Second Amendment over the other will matter to future cases, because the Court sometimes reaches results in gun rights cases that are difficult to justify under any of its previous precedents — the most consistent pattern in this…
items.t: The Supreme Court is about to decide if assault rifle bans can exist

items.title: Let’s hear it for the leftwing echo chamber | Zoe Williams
items.summary:
By chance, I found myself committed to a debate with people whose views I share. It was an eye-opening experience

I was on a panel recently in a church – St Luke’s in Battersea, south London – about the future of the welfare state, except the other panellists booked to speak on the right of politics were unwell and couldn’t come. And so we ended up with an entirely leftwing panel (albeit different shades of the left).

Puckishly, I suggested that I would split my six minutes of allocated speaking time and do three on what the rightwing panellists would have said, had they appeared, and then three on why they are wrong. But I couldn’t get the arguments right. I know they think the current welfare bill is – between our ageing population, our Neets and our dated expectations about what a decent life looks like and whose job it is to ensure you have one – “unsustainable”. I just couldn’t summon the right mix of tough-minded realism and benign resignation to other people’s misery. It wouldn’t come out of my mouth.

Continue reading...
items.t: Let’s hear it for the leftwing echo chamber | Zoe Williams

items.title: PNG’s parliament is voting on ratifying Bougainville independence. A ‘no’ won’t be the end of the story
items.summary:
After more than a century of struggle, Bougainville is moving closer to becoming the world’s newest nation. An autonomous region of Papua New Guinea (PNG) in the northern Solomon Islands chain, Bougainville is taking its next step toward self-determination after a decade-long civil war and a 25-year peace process.

In a 2019 referendum, almost 98% of Bougainvilleans voted for independence. Today the parliament of PNG will begin to vote on ratifying that result.

A “yes” vote in parliament, if it comes, won’t immediately make Bougainville independent. But it will set the legal machinery moving.

Hard questions such as the future of the island’s contentious Panguna mine remain unresolved, but the vote offers a chance to recognise decades of work from the Bougainvillean and PNG sides that have kept the peace process on track.

items.title: Burnham in Brussels: why party politics still defines the UK’s relationship with Europe
items.summary:
Andy Burnham has attended his first EU-UK summit in Brussels with major agreements reached on youth mobility, food exports and carbon emissions. Ultimately though, the prime minister will have understood that this was merely the start of new political negotiations. Back home in the UK, he has started a “national conversation” on the future of UK-EU relations that gained momentum rapidly.

Burnham held talks with European Council president Antonio Costa and president of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen. Both Burnham and Costa come from sister social democratic parties and both are former mayors – Burnham of Greater Manchester and Costa of Lisbon. This could make for smoother meetings in future than in the months and years after the 2016 Brexit referendum.

In the run up to the talks, the prime minister had repeatedly claimed that the Conservatives failed to get a good deal from the EU. As part of former prime minister Keir Starmer’s “reset” of relations with Europe, then-business secretary, Peter Kyle, and European Commission vice-president Teresa Ribera signed a deal committing the UK and the EU to closer cooperation on trade.
